## Definition

An **extraneous variable** is any variable other than the independent variable that could potentially influence the dependent variable. These are unwanted sources of variation that can add "noise" to your data.

## Extraneous vs. Confounding

| Extraneous Variable | Confounding Variable |
|--------------------|---------------------|
| *Might* affect DV | *Does* affect DV |
| Adds random noise | Creates systematic bias |
| Reduces precision | Threatens validity |
| Affects both groups equally | Varies with the IV |

An extraneous variable becomes a **confound** when it systematically varies with the IV.

## Examples

| Study | Possible Extraneous Variables |
|-------|------------------------------|
| Memory test | Room temperature, time of day, noise |
| Reaction time | Caffeine intake, sleep, motivation |
| Therapy outcome | Therapist personality, life events |

## Controlling Extraneous Variables

| Method | How It Works |
|--------|--------------|
| Standardisation | Keep constant across conditions |
| Random assignment | Distribute equally across groups |
| Counterbalancing | Balance order effects |
| Matching | Pair similar participants |
| Statistical control | Include as covariate |

## Example: Standardisation

Testing effect of music on concentration:

| Standardised | Variable |
|--------------|----------|
| Room | Same quiet room for all |
| Time | All tested at same time |
| Instructions | Read from script |
| Breaks | Same duration |
| Equipment | Identical for all |

## When Extraneous Variables Matter

```
High extraneous variation:
├── More noise in data
├── Larger error variance
├── Harder to detect true effects
└── Need larger sample size

Low extraneous variation:
├── Cleaner data
├── Smaller error variance
├── Easier to detect effects
└── More statistical power
```

## DataLab Connection

At the **Reflex Test**, extraneous variables like prior caffeine intake, tiredness, or familiarity with computer tasks could affect reaction times. These add noise but don't systematically favour one condition.
